sm: This is the Franklin Board of Mayor and Aldermen work session for November 24th, 2026. Roll was called, with Alderman Caesar absent, and only two citizen speaker cards were submitted. The board reviewed a contract with the state comptroller for a new annual compliance attestation that the mayor must sign and file by January 1st. Staff then presented draft resolution 2026-104 setting budget goals for fiscal 2028. The foundational goals include a structurally balanced budget, compliance with reserve and debt policies, and timely delivery of the ten-year capital program. Areas of emphasis include fiscal limits from inflation, heavy reliance on sales tax and possible state limits on property tax, attainable housing, and workforce retention.

Staff continued through the remaining areas of emphasis. These include succession planning and training, relationships with Williamson County, the state and federal governments, and infrastructure delivery such as the transit, downtown parking and pedestrian plans, intersection improvements, and planning for the South Clean Water Plant. Service enhancements include biosolid and compost locations, expanded glass recycling, and the effective use of AI. A resolution is planned for the December meeting. Alderman Bagget asked about the housing fund, and staff said this year would only explore how a fund might be structured, not fund it. Alderman Burger asked about ongoing cost savings and innovation, and staff said efficiency measures are built into the budget process. He also asked that employees with great ideas be rewarded.

A board member suggested reviewing the last eighteen years of budget growth. Staff said general fund growth last year was around two percent and all funds around three percent. The ten-year capital program is about 460 million dollars, with only about thirty percent funded by debt and seventy percent from cash. The board then took up the 113 Old Carter's Creek Pike site discussion. Taylor Hopkins of Water Management explained that the city makes Class A exceptional quality biosolids, which could be stored, mixed with compost and sold. Landfilling costs sixty-five dollars a ton for about six thousand tons a year, roughly 360,000 dollars. Three city-owned sites were considered, and he began describing the Ottersgate Way site, where only about four acres sit outside the floodplain.
